lead: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a mathematical model that reads a string symbol by symbol and decides whether the string belongs to a particular language. It exists to give a precise, algorithmic description of regular languages, which appear in lexical analysis, network protocol validation, and simple control logic. DFAs are used in hardware design, text search, and anywhere a fixed‑size controller must recognise patterns quickly.
prereq: You need: Alphabets, strings and formal languages.

blocks.text: A DFA is a 5‑tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F). Q is a finite set of states. Σ is a finite alphabet of input symbols. δ is the transition function that maps a state and an input symbol to a next state, written δ: Q × Σ → Q. q₀ ∈ Q is the start state. F ⊆ Q is the set of accept (final) states.

blocks.where: Q = set of states; Σ = input alphabet; δ = transition function; q₀ = start state; F = accept states

blocks.text: A string w = a₁a₂…aₙ (each aᵢ ∈ Σ) is accepted if the sequence of states q₀, q₁, …, qₙ defined by for i = 0 … n‑1, q_{i+1} = δ(q_i, a_{i+1}) ends in a state belonging to F. The language of the DFA is the set of all accepted strings.

items: States (Q): distinct configurations the machine can be in.
Alphabet (Σ): the symbols the machine reads, e.g., {0,1} for binary strings.
Start state (q₀): the state before any input is read.
Accept states (F): the states that signal successful recognition.
Transition function (δ): a table that tells, for each (state, symbol) pair, which state to move to next.
Look up the pair (current state, symbol) in δ.
Move to the returned next state.
If the final state is in F, accept; otherwise reject.

blocks.text: We design a DFA over the binary alphabet Σ = {0,1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are 01. The idea is to remember the most recent symbols while scanning.

items: Create a start state q₀ meaning “no relevant suffix seen”.
Create state q₁ meaning “the last symbol read was 0”.
Create state q₂ meaning “the last two symbols read were 01”. This will be the only accept state.
• From q₀, on 0 go to q₁; on 1 stay in q₀.
• From q₁, on 0 stay in q₁; on 1 go to q₂.
• From q₂, on 0 go to q₁; on 1 go to q₀.

blocks.text: For the input w = 11001 the DFA visits the states q₀ → q₀ → q₀ → q₁ → q₁ → q₂ and ends in the accept state q₂, so it accepts.

examples.question: Construct a DFA over Σ = {0,1} that accepts all strings whose last two symbols are 01. Show the state diagram, transition table, and trace the DFA on the input w = 11001.
steps: Define three states: q0 (start), q1 (last symbol was 0), q2 (last two symbols were 01).
Write the transition function δ as described in the design steps.
Draw the state diagram (see the figure).
Final state is q2, which is accepting.
examples.answer: The DFA has three states q0, q1, q2 with q2 as the only accept state; on w = 11001 it ends in q2, therefore the string is accepted.

traps: Assuming the transition function can be partial; δ must be defined for every state‑symbol pair.
Treating the accept state as a start state; the start state is always q₀, not any accept state.
Confusing the order of symbols when tracing; the DFA reads left‑to‑right, not right‑to‑left.
Including extra states that are never reachable; they increase the DFA size without changing the language.

quiz.q: What does the symbol δ represent in a DFA?
quiz.a: The transition function that maps a state and an input symbol to the next state.

quiz.q: List the five components of the 5‑tuple that defines a DFA.
quiz.a: Q (states), Σ (alphabet), δ (transition function), q₀ (start state), F (set of accept states).

quiz.q: Explain why a DFA cannot have two different transitions for the same state‑symbol pair.
quiz.a: Because the machine is deterministic; at any step there must be exactly one next state, otherwise the computation would be ambiguous.

quiz.q: Using the transition table from the example, determine whether the string 0010 is accepted.
quiz.a: Trace: q0→q1 (0) →q1 (0) →q1 (1) →q0 (0). Final state q0 is not accepting, so the string is rejected.

quiz.q: Draw the state diagram for a DFA that accepts all strings that contain the substring 11.
quiz.a: Three states: q0 (no 1 seen), q1 (last symbol was 1), q2 (substring 11 seen, accept). Transitions: q0‑0→q0, q0‑1→q1; q1‑0→q0, q1‑1→q2; q2‑0→q2, q2‑1→q2.

quiz.q: A student claims that adding a self‑loop on the start state for both symbols does not change the language of the DFA in the example. Is the claim correct? Justify.
quiz.a: The claim is false. Adding a self‑loop on q0 for symbol 0 would keep the machine in q0 after reading a 0, losing the memory of a trailing 0 needed to recognise the suffix 01. The language would become the empty set because the accept state q2 could never be reached.

quiz.q: Compare a DFA and an NFA in terms of the transition function definition.
quiz.a: In a DFA, δ maps each (state, symbol) to exactly one next state. In an NFA, the transition relation can map a pair to a set of possible next states, allowing zero, one, or many choices.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, DFAs appear in hardware description languages for designing finite‑state controllers, such as traffic‑light sequencers or packet‑filter firewalls. Research extends DFAs to weighted automata for speech recognition and to streaming algorithms for real‑time intrusion detection. Modern curricula link DFAs to model checking, where state‑space exploration uses similar transition systems. Next, explore NFA and learn how nondeterminism simplifies design while preserving expressive power.
